subject: selective
title: Reading comprehension · Test 1
summary: A 30-minute practice reading test with four original passages (including a poem) and 30 multiple-choice questions on main idea, inference, vocabulary, tone and poetry.
body:
Read the four passages below, then answer the 30 questions. You have 30 minutes. Each question names the passage it is about. Look back at the passage for every answer — the evidence is always there in the text.

## Passage A — The Night Market

Every Thursday, Mei's grandmother set up her dumpling stall in the far corner of the night market, between a man who sold phone cases and a van that smelled of burnt sugar. Mei had helped for three years now. She knew how to fold the paper boxes, how to count change from a fifty, and how to smile at customers even when her feet ached.

Her grandmother, Po Po, did not smile much. She worked with her head down, pinching each dumpling closed with exactly seven pleats. When Mei had once tried to do it with five, Po Po had silently unpicked it and handed it back.

That Thursday the sky turned the colour of a bruise just after six o'clock. The wind arrived first, snatching napkins off tables and sending a stack of paper boxes cartwheeling across the car park. Then the rain came sideways.

All around them, stallholders were dragging down their awnings. The phone-case man had already gone, leaving a single cable coiled on the asphalt. Mei grabbed the corner of the tarpaulin as it lifted, and held on.

"Leave it," Po Po said. "Get the steamers."

Mei wanted to argue — the tarp would blow away, and then what? — but something in her grandmother's voice made her let go. Together they lifted the bamboo steamers, still hot, into the plastic tubs and snapped the lids on. The tarp flapped twice, tore free and sailed over the fence.

By the time the storm had passed, the market was half empty. A queue of soaked, hungry people had gathered at the only stall still able to serve hot food. Po Po lit the burner again. Her hands, Mei noticed, were shaking, but not from cold.

They sold out in forty minutes.

Driving home, Po Po said nothing for a long time. Then, at a red light, she reached across and squeezed Mei's hand, once, hard.

"Tarpaulins are cheap," she said.

Mei looked out at the wet streets shining under the streetlights and understood that this was the closest her grandmother would come to saying thank you. It was, she decided, close enough.

## Passage B — Dancing Directions

Imagine trying to give a friend directions to a café without words, a map or a phone — and doing it in complete darkness. Honeybees solve this problem every day, and they do it by dancing.

When a forager bee finds a rich patch of flowers, she flies back to the hive and performs what scientists call the waggle dance on the upright wall of the honeycomb. She runs forward in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side, then loops back to her starting point and runs the straight line again, curving back the other way each time. From above, her path looks like a figure eight with a wobbly line through the middle.

The straight "waggle run" is the important part. Its direction tells the other bees which way to fly. Inside the dark hive, straight up the comb stands for the direction of the sun. If the waggle run points straight up, the flowers are in the same direction as the sun. If it points 40 degrees to the right of straight up, the flowers lie 40 degrees to the right of the sun. The length of time the bee spends waggling tells how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the longer the flight.

The other bees cannot see the dance in the dark. Instead, they crowd close and follow the dancer, feeling her movements with their antennae. They also pick up the scent of the flowers clinging to her body, which helps them recognise the right blossoms when they arrive.

The dance even allows for time passing. The sun moves across the sky during the day, and bees seem to adjust the angle of their dances to match, so the directions stay correct hours later.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent many years puzzling over these movements before he worked out what they meant, and he later shared a Nobel Prize for his work on animal behaviour. Some scientists at first refused to believe that an insect could pass on such precise information. Later experiments, including some using tiny robot bees, helped convince the doubters.

Not every dance is equally lively. A bee returning from an excellent food source dances with more energy, and repeats her dance many more times, than one returning from a poor patch. In this way the hive sends more workers to the best flowers without any single bee being in charge.

Next time you see a bee on a flower, remember: she might be about to fly home and draw a map with her body.

## Passage C — First Tram

The city hasn't brushed its hair,  
the streetlights blink and yawn;  
I stand beside the empty rails  
and wait to catch the dawn.

A pigeon checks the bins for crumbs,  
a cleaner drags a hose,  
the bakery across the road  
breathes warmth against my nose.

Then far away, a silver hum,  
a rattle in the ground —  
the first tram shoulders through the dark  
and gathers up the sound.

It opens like a lighted room,  
it does not ask me why;  
I climb aboard, and all the town  
wakes slowly, passing by.

## Passage D — Letter to the school newsletter

To the Editor,

Last week the school announced that, from next term, the library will be closed at lunchtime so that staff can do stocktake and book repairs. I understand that these jobs matter. But I am writing to ask the school to think again, because for many students the lunchtime library is far more than a room full of books.

For a start, not everyone enjoys a noisy, crowded yard. Some students are new to the school and have not found their group yet. Others simply need forty minutes of quiet to recharge before afternoon classes. The library gives all of them somewhere safe to be.

Secondly, the library is where many of us finish homework, print assignments and borrow laptops. Students without a printer or a quiet space at home depend on it. Closing it at lunch makes school harder for exactly the students who already have the least help.

Some people say students can simply visit before or after school. However, many of us catch buses that arrive just before the bell and leave straight after it. For these students, lunchtime is the only time the library is open to them at all.

I am not asking the library staff to give up their repair work. Student volunteers — and I would be first in line — could help with simple jobs like covering books and shelving, freeing up staff time. A shared problem can have a shared solution.

Please keep our library doors open at lunch. A school that says it cares about every student should keep open the one room where every student is welcome.

Yours sincerely,
Priya Nair, Year 8

questions.prompt: In Passage A, why does Po Po tell Mei to leave the tarpaulin?

options.A: She thinks the tarpaulin is too heavy and the wind too strong for Mei to hold it safely.
options.B: She judges that saving the steamers and food matters more than saving the cover.
options.C: She wants to close the stall and go home early.
options.D: She knows the phone-case man will bring it back later.

questions.explanation: Po Po says "Get the steamers" instead, the food is saved, they sell out, and later she says "Tarpaulins are cheap" — the cover was less valuable than the food. Nothing suggests the tarp was too heavy; that reason is made up.
steps: Find what Po Po says straight after 'Leave it': 'Get the steamers.' She is choosing the steamers over the tarp.
Check later evidence: they keep serving hot food and sell out, and Po Po says 'Tarpaulins are cheap.'
So she left the cheap cover because the steamers and food mattered more.

mistakes.A: Trap: inventing a reason. The passage never says the tarp was too heavy — look at what Po Po tells Mei to do instead, and at what she says in the car.
mistakes.C: Trap: ignoring later evidence. Po Po lights the burner again and keeps selling, so she did not want to go home. Read on to the end before deciding.
mistakes.D: Trap: a detail from the wrong place. The phone-case man had already left; nothing links him to the tarp. Stick to what the text supports.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, the sky 'turned the colour of a bruise'. This suggests the sky was

options.A: dark purple-grey, warning that a storm was coming.
options.B: bright orange and red from a beautiful sunset.
options.C: pale blue and clear.
options.D: so painful that Mei could not look at it.

questions.explanation: A bruise is dark purple and grey, and the very next sentences describe wind and sideways rain, so the colour signals a storm. A sunset is a tempting picture for 'just after six', but bruises are not bright orange.
steps: Picture a bruise: it is dark purple, blue-grey and yellowish — dull, heavy colours.
Read on: the wind and sideways rain arrive straight away.
So the sky was dark purple-grey, warning of the storm.

mistakes.B: Trap: picturing the time of day instead of the comparison. Think about what colour a bruise actually is, and what happens next in the story.
mistakes.C: Trap: ignoring the comparison. A bruise is not pale blue, and a clear sky does not fit the wind and rain that follow.
mistakes.D: Trap: reading a comparison literally. The sky cannot hurt; the writer compares only its colour to a bruise.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, Po Po's hands were shaking, 'but not from cold'. This most likely suggests that

options.A: she was ill and should not have been working.
options.B: she was angry with Mei for letting go of the tarp.
options.C: the storm had shaken her up more than she let anyone see.
options.D: the gas burner was too hot to touch safely.

questions.explanation: The writer rules out cold, so the shaking comes from feeling: the storm and the rush to save the stall had shaken her, even though she shows little emotion. Anger at Mei cannot be right because Po Po told her to let go.
steps: The writer says the shaking is 'not from cold', so look for another cause in the story.
Po Po has just been through a sudden storm and nearly lost her stall, yet she 'did not smile much' and hides her feelings.
So the shaking shows the storm upset or stressed her more than she let show.

mistakes.A: Trap: jumping to an extreme idea. Nothing in the passage mentions illness; think about what had just happened in the storm.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing the instruction. Po Po herself told Mei to 'Leave it', so she could not be angry about it — and later she squeezes Mei's hand.
mistakes.D: Trap: grabbing a nearby detail. The burner is mentioned just before, but heat from a burner does not make hands shake.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best states the main idea of Passage A?

options.A: A sudden storm can wreck a market stall in minutes.
options.B: Mei learns to fold dumplings with exactly seven pleats.
options.C: Running a night-market stall is a risky way to earn a living, because bad weather can ruin a whole night.
options.D: A grandmother who rarely shows her feelings finds a quiet way to show she values her granddaughter.

questions.explanation: The story builds to Po Po squeezing Mei's hand and Mei understanding it is a thank-you, so the main idea is about their relationship. The storm is only the event that reveals it.
steps: Ask: where does the story end up? Po Po squeezes Mei's hand and Mei sees it as a thank-you.
Ask: what has the whole story shown about Po Po? She is quiet and strict, and rarely shows feelings.
The main idea joins these: a reserved grandmother quietly shows she values Mei.

mistakes.A: Trap: choosing the main event instead of the main idea. The storm is what happens, but the story is about what it shows between Mei and Po Po.
mistakes.B: Trap: a small detail. The pleats appear in one sentence to show Po Po's character; they are not what the whole story is about.
mistakes.C: Trap: a big general statement the passage does not argue. The story is about two people, not about market businesses in general.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, what does the detail about Po Po unpicking Mei's five-pleat dumpling mainly show?

options.A: Po Po does not want Mei to help at the stall.
options.B: Mei is lazy and careless, so Po Po has to check and redo almost everything she makes.
options.C: Po Po has high standards and tends to say things through actions rather than words.
options.D: Dumplings with fewer than seven pleats always burst when cooked.

questions.explanation: Po Po fixes the dumpling 'silently' — she is exact about her work and shows it without speaking, just as she later thanks Mei with a squeeze instead of words. Mei has helped for three years, so Po Po does want her help.
steps: Notice the key words: 'exactly seven pleats' and 'silently unpicked it'.
'Exactly' shows high standards; 'silently' shows she acts instead of talking.
So the detail shows a demanding grandmother who communicates through actions.

mistakes.A: Trap: ignoring the bigger picture. Mei has helped for three years, so Po Po clearly lets her help; the unpicking is about how things are done.
mistakes.B: Trap: reading too much into one moment. One try with five pleats does not make Mei lazy — she knows many jobs at the stall.
mistakes.D: Trap: bringing in outside 'facts'. The passage never says why seven pleats are needed; keep to what the text tells you.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes the tone of the final paragraph of Passage A ('Mei looked out … close enough')?

options.A: Bitterly disappointed
options.B: Quietly content
options.C: Wildly excited
options.D: Nervous and uneasy

questions.explanation: Mei accepts the hand squeeze as a thank-you and decides it is 'close enough' — a calm, satisfied ending. 'Disappointed' is tempting because she knows Po Po will never say the words, but she is at peace with that.
steps: Find the feeling words: Mei 'understood' and 'decided … close enough'.
'Close enough' means she accepts it and is satisfied, and the calm streets match this.
So the tone is quietly content.

mistakes.A: Trap: stopping halfway through the paragraph. 'The closest her grandmother would come' sounds sad, but the last sentence says it was 'close enough'.
mistakes.C: Trap: overstating. Mei is pleased, but the calm picture of shining streets and the short last line are gentle, not wild.
mistakes.D: Trap: carrying over the storm's mood. The danger has passed; nothing in this paragraph shows worry.

questions.prompt: Near the end of Passage A, Po Po says, "Tarpaulins are cheap." What is she really telling Mei?

options.A: That losing the tarp did not matter, because what they saved together mattered far more.
options.B: That she plans to buy a better tarpaulin next week.
options.C: That Mei should pay for the tarpaulin she let blow away.
options.D: That the stall makes so much money that losing equipment in a storm never really matters to her.

questions.explanation: Said while squeezing Mei's hand after a successful night, the line means: the cheap tarp was not important; saving the steamers (and Mei's trust in her) was. Mei takes it as 'the closest … to saying thank you'. The 'buy a new one' reading takes the words too literally.
steps: Look at the moment: Po Po squeezes Mei's hand, then speaks.
Remember the choice they made: let the tarp go, save the steamers — and they sold out.
So she means the tarp didn't matter; what they saved together did — her way of thanking Mei.

mistakes.B: Trap: reading the words only at face value. Think about why she says this right after squeezing Mei's hand, not about shopping.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing the mood. Po Po told Mei to let it go and has just squeezed her hand; she is not blaming her.
mistakes.D: Trap: turning one remark into a big claim. She is talking about this night, not saying money never matters.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, the wind is described as 'snatching napkins off tables'. This is an example of

options.A: a simile — comparing two things using 'like' or 'as'.
options.B: onomatopoeia — a word that sounds like its meaning.
options.C: personification — giving the wind a human action.
options.D: rhyme — words with matching end sounds.

questions.explanation: Snatching is something a person (or animal) does with hands; giving that action to the wind is personification. It is not a simile because there is no 'like' or 'as'.
steps: Ask: who usually 'snatches'? A person, with their hands.
Here the wind is doing it, so a human action is given to something non-human.
That is personification.

mistakes.A: Trap: naming the wrong device. Look for 'like' or 'as' in the phrase; there isn't one.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing devices. 'Snatching' describes an action; it does not imitate a sound.
mistakes.D: Trap: confusing devices. No words in the phrase rhyme with each other.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage B?

options.A: To persuade readers to protect honeybees
options.B: To explain how honeybees use a dance to tell other bees where food is
options.C: To tell the life story of Karl von Frisch
options.D: To entertain readers with a made-up story about a bee

questions.explanation: Almost every paragraph explains part of the waggle dance — direction, distance, how bees follow it — so the purpose is to explain. It does not try to persuade, so 'protect honeybees' is wrong.
steps: Look at what each paragraph does: describe the dance, explain direction and distance, explain how bees follow it.
There is no argument or request, so it is not persuasive.
So its purpose is to explain how bees use the dance to show where food is.

mistakes.A: Trap: guessing the purpose from the topic. The passage never argues or asks readers to do anything; it explains.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing one paragraph. Von Frisch appears in just one paragraph; most of the passage is about the dance.
mistakes.D: Trap: wrong text type. This is factual writing with no characters or plot.

questions.prompt: According to Passage B, how do the bees inside the hive follow the dance?

options.A: They feel the dancer's movements with their antennae.
options.B: They watch her closely in the light near the entrance.
options.C: They listen carefully to the buzzing of her wings.
options.D: They follow a scent trail she leaves across the comb.

questions.explanation: The passage says the bees 'cannot see the dance in the dark' and instead feel her movements 'with their antennae'. Scent is mentioned, but only for recognising the right flowers.
steps: Find the paragraph about following the dance: 'The other bees cannot see the dance in the dark.'
The next sentence says they crowd close, 'feeling her movements with their antennae.'
So they follow it by touch, with their antennae.

mistakes.B: Trap: ignoring a key fact. The passage says the dance happens in the dark and the bees 'cannot see' it.
mistakes.C: Trap: guessing from general knowledge. Sound is not mentioned in the passage; find the sentence that explains how they follow.
mistakes.D: Trap: twisting a real detail. Scent is mentioned, but it helps bees recognise the flowers later, not follow the dance.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, a bee's waggle run points 60 degrees to the left of straight up. Where are the flowers?

options.A: 60 degrees to the right of the direction of the sun
options.B: 60 metres to the left of the hive
options.C: Straight towards the sun, 60 times farther away
options.D: 60 degrees to the left of the direction of the sun

questions.explanation: Straight up stands for the sun's direction, and the angle from straight up equals the angle from the sun on the same side (the passage's example: 40° right means 40° right of the sun). So 60° left means 60° left of the sun.
steps: Straight up the comb stands for the direction of the sun.
The angle of the waggle run from straight up equals the angle of the food from the sun, on the same side.
So 60° left of straight up means the flowers are 60° to the left of the sun.

mistakes.A: Trap: flipping the direction. The passage's example keeps the same side: right of straight up means right of the sun, so left means left.
mistakes.B: Trap: mixing up angle and distance. The angle gives direction; distance comes from how long the bee waggles.
mistakes.C: Trap: misusing the number. The 60 is an angle, not a distance or a multiple.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, Bee X waggles for 4 seconds on each run and Bee Y waggles for 1 second. What can you conclude?

options.A: Bee X's food is better quality than Bee Y's.
options.B: Bee Y's food is farther from the hive than Bee X's.
options.C: Bee X's food is farther from the hive than Bee Y's.
options.D: Bee X is more tired than Bee Y.

questions.explanation: The passage says 'the longer the waggle, the longer the flight', so the 4-second waggle means a farther food source. Quality is a different signal — energy and repeats — so 'better quality' cannot be concluded.
steps: Find what the length of the waggle tells: 'the longer the waggle, the longer the flight.'
Bee X waggles longer (4 s) than Bee Y (1 s).
So Bee X's food is farther away; nothing here tells us about quality.

mistakes.A: Trap: mixing up two clues. Quality is shown by how lively the dance is and how often it is repeated, not by how long each waggle lasts.
mistakes.B: Trap: reversing the rule. Re-read: 'the longer the waggle, the longer the flight.'
mistakes.D: Trap: inventing a reason. The passage never links waggle time to tiredness; it links it to distance.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, robot bees 'helped convince the doubters'. In this sentence, 'doubters' are

options.A: people who had proved von Frisch wrong
options.B: bees that refused to follow the dance
options.C: people who were not sure the idea was true
options.D: the scientists who built the robot bees

questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'some scientists at first refused to believe' the idea; those are the doubters — people who were unsure or unconvinced. They had not proved von Frisch wrong; they were later convinced.
steps: Look at the sentence just before: some scientists 'refused to believe' an insect could pass on precise information.
'Doubters' points back to those unconvinced people.
So doubters are people who were not sure the idea was true.

mistakes.A: Trap: making the word too strong. A doubter is unsure; they had not proved anything, and were later convinced.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing who the sentence is about. The sentence before talks about 'some scientists' who 'refused to believe'.
mistakes.D: Trap: mixing up the people. The robot bees were used to convince the doubters, so the builders were not the doubters.

questions.prompt: Why does Passage B begin by asking readers to imagine giving directions in the dark without words?

options.A: To link the bees' problem to a human experience, so readers see how impressive the dance is
options.B: To suggest that humans are much worse at sharing directions than bees are, even with maps and phones
options.C: To give instructions for finding a café
options.D: To show that the writer is unsure how bees communicate

questions.explanation: The opening makes readers feel how hard it would be for them, then reveals bees do it every day — this hooks the reader and shows the dance is remarkable. It never claims humans are worse communicators.
steps: Notice the opening asks 'Imagine…' — the reader pictures a hard task themselves.
The next sentence: 'Honeybees solve this problem every day.'
So it links to human experience to show how impressive the bees' dance is.

mistakes.B: Trap: overstating. The opening makes the bees' task feel hard and clever, but never says humans are worse.
mistakes.C: Trap: reading the example literally. The café is just an everyday example for the reader to imagine.
mistakes.D: Trap: misreading the opening. The writer goes on to explain the dance confidently.

questions.prompt: Which statement would the writer of Passage B most likely agree with?

options.A: Von Frisch's explanation was accepted straight away by all scientists.
options.B: Bees can find food only at the exact moment the dance is performed.
options.C: A hive can make good group choices even though no single bee is in charge.
options.D: Only the queen bee can understand the waggle dance.

questions.explanation: The last paragraph says lively dances send 'more workers to the best flowers without any single bee being in charge' — a group choice. Von Frisch's idea was doubted at first, so 'accepted straight away' is contradicted.
steps: Test each option against the passage.
The paragraph on lively dances ends: the hive sends more workers to the best flowers 'without any single bee being in charge'.
So the writer would agree that the hive makes good group choices with no single leader.

mistakes.A: Trap: missing a contradiction. The passage says some scientists 'at first refused to believe'.
mistakes.B: Trap: ignoring a detail. The passage says bees adjust the angle so 'the directions stay correct hours later'.
mistakes.D: Trap: adding outside ideas. The queen is never mentioned; ordinary bees crowd round and follow.

questions.prompt: Passage B ends by saying a bee might 'draw a map with her body'. Which detail from the passage best supports calling the dance a 'map'?

options.A: From above, the dance looks like a figure eight.
options.B: The dancer carries the scent of the flowers.
options.C: Better food sources produce livelier dances.
options.D: The dance shows both the direction and the distance of the food.

questions.explanation: A map tells you which way to go and how far — exactly what the angle (direction) and waggle length (distance) do. The figure-eight shape is tempting because 'draw' suggests a picture, but the shape alone gives no location.
steps: Ask: what does a map tell you? Which way to go and how far.
The passage: the angle gives direction, and the waggle time gives distance.
So the detail that supports 'map' is that the dance shows direction and distance.

mistakes.A: Trap: matching the shape, not the job. A map's job is to show where things are; a figure-eight shape does not do that by itself.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing finding with recognising. Scent helps bees recognise flowers on arrival, not know where to go.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing a detail about quality. A map shows location, not how good a place is.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, 'It opens like a lighted room' is an example of

options.A: a metaphor
options.B: onomatopoeia
options.C: a simile
options.D: alliteration

questions.explanation: The line compares the tram to a lighted room using 'like', so it is a simile. A metaphor would say the tram 'is' a lighted room.
steps: Look for 'like' or 'as': the line says 'like a lighted room'.
A comparison using 'like' or 'as' is a simile.
So the line is a simile.

mistakes.A: Trap: missing the signal word. A metaphor says something IS something else; this line uses 'like'.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing devices. None of these words imitates a sound.
mistakes.D: Trap: confusing devices. Alliteration needs several nearby words starting with the same sound; these do not.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, what time of day is it, and how can you tell?

options.A: Very early morning — the speaker waits 'to catch the dawn' for the 'first tram'.
options.B: Late at night — because the streetlights are still on and the rails are completely empty.
options.C: Evening peak hour — because the speaker is going home.
options.D: Midday — because the bakery is busy.

questions.explanation: The speaker waits 'to catch the dawn', the title says 'First Tram', and the town 'wakes slowly' — all point to very early morning. Streetlights alone could mean night, but the dawn and the first tram settle it.
steps: Gather clues: 'wait to catch the dawn', the title 'First Tram', the town 'wakes slowly'.
Dark plus dawn plus the first tram of the day means just before sunrise.
So it is very early morning.

mistakes.B: Trap: using half the evidence. Streetlights are on before dawn too; check what the speaker is waiting for.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing details. There are no crowds and the rails are 'empty'; nothing says the speaker is going home.
mistakes.D: Trap: ignoring the darkness. The tram comes 'through the dark', so it cannot be midday.

questions.prompt: In the third stanza of Passage C, the tram 'shoulders through the dark'. 'Shoulders' suggests the tram

options.A: carries passengers on its roof
options.B: pushes its way forward strongly, like a person through a crowd
options.C: moves gently and silently
options.D: turns sideways around a corner

questions.explanation: To 'shoulder through' is to push forward with force, as you might through a crowd — the tram forces its way through the darkness. It is not gentle: the stanza has a hum and a rattle.
steps: Think of a person 'shouldering through' a crowd: they push firmly forward.
The tram does this 'through the dark', with a hum and a rattle.
So 'shoulders' means it pushes strongly forward.

mistakes.A: Trap: taking the word literally, as in carrying something on your shoulders. Think of 'shouldering through' a crowd.
mistakes.C: Trap: ignoring the sound clues. The stanza mentions a 'hum' and a 'rattle', and 'shoulders' suggests force.
mistakes.D: Trap: picturing a body turning. Nothing in the stanza mentions a corner; focus on the forceful movement.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the rhyme pattern in each stanza of Passage C?

options.A: Every pair of lines rhymes (first with second, third with fourth).
options.B: The first and third lines rhyme.
options.C: None of the lines rhyme.
options.D: Only the second and fourth lines rhyme.

questions.explanation: In stanza 1, 'yawn' rhymes with 'dawn' (lines 2 and 4) but 'hair' and 'rails' do not; the same pattern holds in every stanza (hose/nose, ground/sound, why/by). Couplets would need 'hair' to rhyme with 'yawn'.
steps: List the line endings of stanza 1: hair, yawn, rails, dawn.
Only yawn/dawn rhyme. Check the others: hose/nose, ground/sound, why/by.
So only the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme.

mistakes.A: Trap: not checking the line endings. 'Hair' and 'yawn' do not rhyme.
mistakes.B: Trap: checking the wrong lines. 'Hair' and 'rails' do not rhyme; look at lines 2 and 4.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing the rhyme. 'Yawn' and 'dawn' clearly rhyme.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best describes the main idea of Passage C?

options.A: The speaker is annoyed that the tram is so late.
options.B: A quiet, sleepy city slowly comes to life as the speaker begins the day on the first tram.
options.C: Cities are dirty, empty and lonely places early in the morning, before anyone else is awake.
options.D: The poem explains how electric trams work.

questions.explanation: The poem moves from a city that 'hasn't brushed its hair' to the town that 'wakes slowly' as the tram carries the speaker — a city coming to life at the start of the day. Nothing suggests annoyance.
steps: Compare the start and end: the city is sleepy ('blink and yawn'), then 'wakes slowly'.
The tram is what carries the speaker into the waking day.
So the main idea is the sleepy city coming to life as the speaker's day begins.

mistakes.A: Trap: inventing a feeling. Waiting is mentioned, but nothing shows annoyance; the ending is peaceful.
mistakes.C: Trap: over-reading small details. Bins and empty rails appear, but the bakery's warmth and the welcoming tram are not lonely or grim.
mistakes.D: Trap: confusing a detail with the purpose. The 'silver hum' describes a sound; the poem does not explain machines.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes the speaker's mood in the final stanza of Passage C?

options.A: Lonely and afraid
options.B: Impatient and irritable
options.C: Sorry and regretful
options.D: Calm and welcomed

questions.explanation: A 'lighted room' that 'does not ask me why' feels warm and accepting, and the town waking 'slowly' is gentle — the speaker feels calm and welcomed. 'Lonely' is tempting because it is early and quiet, but the images are warm.
steps: Find the images: 'like a lighted room', 'does not ask me why', 'wakes slowly'.
A lit room is warm and inviting; not being questioned feels accepting.
So the mood is calm and welcomed.

mistakes.A: Trap: misreading 'it does not ask me why' as cold. The tram 'opens like a lighted room' — a warm, inviting picture.
mistakes.B: Trap: carrying over the idea of waiting. By this stanza the waiting is over and the speaker climbs aboard.
mistakes.C: Trap: no evidence. Nothing in the stanza looks back with regret.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, the tram 'does not ask me why'. This line most likely suggests that

options.A: the tram accepts the speaker without questions, which feels comforting so early in the day
options.B: the speaker has done something wrong and is hiding it
options.C: the tram driver is rude and ignores the passengers, not even asking where they want to go today
options.D: the speaker does not know why they are travelling

questions.explanation: The tram is personified as a host who simply lets the speaker in — no questions — which goes with the warm 'lighted room'. Reading it as rudeness ignores that warm image.
steps: The line gives the tram a human action (asking questions) — personification.
It comes right after 'It opens like a lighted room', a warm, welcoming image.
So it suggests the tram accepts the speaker without questions, which feels comforting.

mistakes.B: Trap: over-reading. Nothing in the poem hints at a secret or guilt.
mistakes.C: Trap: reading it as a complaint. The tram is described as a 'lighted room', a welcoming picture.
mistakes.D: Trap: switching who is asking. The line is about the tram not asking, not about the speaker being unsure.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose in Passage D?

options.A: To complain about the library staff
options.B: To tell students when stocktake will happen
options.C: To ask the school to buy more laptops
options.D: To persuade the school to keep the library open at lunchtime

questions.explanation: The letter gives reasons and ends with 'Please keep our library doors open at lunch' — it is persuading. It does not complain about staff; it offers volunteers to help them.
steps: Look at the request at the end: 'Please keep our library doors open at lunch.'
The paragraphs before give reasons supporting that request.
So the purpose is to persuade the school to keep the library open at lunch.

mistakes.A: Trap: misreading the tone. The writer supports the staff's work and offers to help them.
mistakes.B: Trap: choosing a detail. Stocktake is mentioned only as the reason for the change.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing a detail. Laptops are one example of what the library offers.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, which sentence is the writer's reply to an argument against her view?

options.A: "However, many of us catch buses that arrive just before the bell and leave straight after it."
options.B: "Closing it at lunch makes school harder for exactly the students who already have the least help."
options.C: "Please keep our library doors open at lunch."
options.D: "The library gives all of them somewhere safe to be."

questions.explanation: The paragraph starts with what 'some people say' (visit before or after school), and 'However…' answers it — that is a rebuttal. 'For a start…' is her own first reason, not a reply.
steps: Find where the writer mentions what other people think: 'Some people say students can simply visit before or after school.'
The next sentence begins 'However' and answers that idea with the bus problem.
So the reply is the 'However, many of us catch buses…' sentence.

mistakes.B: Trap: choosing one of her own reasons. This sentence finishes her second argument; it does not answer anyone else's point.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing her final request. This is her call to action, not a reply to an opposing idea.
mistakes.D: Trap: choosing a supporting point. This backs up her first reason; no opposing view is being answered.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, some students 'need forty minutes of quiet to recharge'. Here 'recharge' means

options.A: plug in their phones or laptops
options.B: rest and get their energy back
options.C: pay a fee again
options.D: run around and burn off energy

questions.explanation: The students need 'quiet … before afternoon classes', so recharge means rest and restore their energy. 'Plug in devices' is the usual meaning but does not fit students needing quiet.
steps: Look at who recharges: the students, not devices.
They need 'quiet' before afternoon classes — rest, not activity.
So 'recharge' means rest and get their energy back.

mistakes.A: Trap: the everyday meaning. Laptops are mentioned later, but here 'recharge' is about the students themselves.
mistakes.C: Trap: a different meaning of 'charge'. Nothing about money appears in this paragraph.
mistakes.D: Trap: the opposite idea. The writer says they need 'quiet', not activity.

questions.prompt: According to the writer of Passage D, which students would the lunchtime closure hurt most?

options.A: Students who like playing sport at lunch
options.B: The library staff
options.C: Students who live close to school
options.D: Students who do not have a printer or a quiet place to study at home

questions.explanation: The writer says closing the library 'makes school harder for exactly the students who already have the least help' — those without a printer or quiet space at home. Students who live nearby could visit before or after school, so they are hurt least.
steps: Find the sentence about who is hurt: 'harder for exactly the students who already have the least help.'
The sentence before names them: 'Students without a printer or a quiet space at home.'
So those students would be hurt most.

mistakes.A: Trap: choosing the wrong group. Students in the yard are not the ones who need the library.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing students and staff. The question asks about students, and the closure is meant to help staff.
mistakes.C: Trap: reversing the bus argument. It is students who catch buses, often from further away, who cannot use the library before or after school.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, how does the writer make her suggestion in the fifth paragraph more convincing?

options.A: She uses statistics from other schools to prove that student volunteers can do library work well.
options.B: She threatens that students will stop using the library.
options.C: She offers to help personally, so she is giving a solution and not just complaining.
options.D: She quotes an expert on school libraries.

questions.explanation: 'I would be first in line' shows she will do the work herself, and she suggests volunteers to free up staff time — a practical solution. There are no statistics in the paragraph.
steps: Re-read the fifth paragraph: volunteers could cover books and shelve — 'and I would be first in line'.
Offering your own help shows you are serious and solving the problem, not just complaining.
So she makes it convincing by personally offering a solution.

mistakes.A: Trap: assuming evidence that isn't there. The paragraph has no numbers or survey results.
mistakes.B: Trap: misreading the tone. The paragraph is cooperative; there is no threat.
mistakes.D: Trap: assuming a technique. No expert or quotation appears in the letter.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of Passage D mainly persuades by

options.A: ending with a joke to keep the mood light
options.B: holding the school to its own claim that it cares about every student
options.C: repeating the facts about stocktake from the first paragraph
options.D: admitting her argument might be wrong

questions.explanation: 'A school that says it cares about every student should…' uses the school's own values to make closing the library look inconsistent. It is serious, not a joke.
steps: Look at the words 'a school that says it cares about every student'.
The writer argues that if the school believes this, it should keep the welcoming room open.
So she persuades by holding the school to its own stated value.

mistakes.A: Trap: misjudging the tone. The sentence is serious and direct, not funny.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing what is new. The sentence says nothing about stocktake or repairs.
mistakes.D: Trap: misreading the ending. It is confident, not doubtful.

questions.prompt: Which new piece of information would most WEAKEN the argument in Passage D?

options.A: Almost no students use the library at lunchtime now.
options.B: Student volunteers say they would enjoy covering books.
options.C: The yard is very crowded and noisy at lunch.
options.D: Many students catch buses that arrive just before the bell.

questions.explanation: Her whole argument is that many students need the lunchtime library; if almost nobody uses it, that claim collapses. Each other option backs up one of her reasons.
steps: Find what her argument depends on: lots of students needing the library at lunch.
Check each option: three of them support her reasons.
Only 'almost no students use it now' attacks her main claim, so it weakens the argument most.

mistakes.B: Trap: not checking the direction. This supports her volunteer idea, making her argument stronger.
mistakes.C: Trap: not checking the direction. This supports her first reason, so it strengthens the argument.
mistakes.D: Trap: not checking the direction. This is her own reply to the 'before or after school' idea, so it strengthens her case.
